subject: PHS
vignette: A physician enters the exam room to begin a new patient visit. The patient is seated on the exam table. The physician stands by the door, looks at the chart, and says, "Mr. Johnson, I see you're here for back pain, correct?"
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate way for the physician to begin this encounter?

options.text: Remain standing by the door to convey efficiency and begin reviewing the chart aloud
Address the patient as "Mr. Johnson" since the chart lists his legal name
Sit at eye level near the patient, face the patient directly, and ask how they would like to be addressed
Open with a closed-ended question confirming the chief complaint to keep the visit on schedule
Begin with a detailed review of systems so that fewer follow-up questions are needed later

explanation_correct: The introduction step of patient-centered interviewing requires the physician to introduce themselves and ask the patient's name and how they would like to be addressed, then use the name and pronouns given while avoiding gender assumptions. The physician should also sit at eye level, near the patient, facing them directly, which establishes rapport and equal footing. Opening the encounter this way invites the patient to identify their own concerns rather than having an agenda imposed from the chart.

explanation_incorrect.A: Standing at a distance while reading the chart undermines the introduction step; the physician should sit at eye level, near the patient, facing them directly.
explanation_incorrect.B: Using the name from the chart without asking how the patient wishes to be addressed risks an incorrect or unwanted form of address; the physician should ask and then use the name and pronouns given.
explanation_incorrect.D: Opening with a closed-ended confirmation of the chart's chief complaint skips the introduction and pre-empts agenda setting, in which the patient helps identify their own concerns.
explanation_incorrect.E: Starting with a detailed review of systems is not part of the introduction; the encounter should begin by establishing the patient's identity and preferred address and by inviting their concerns.

educationalObjective: Begin each encounter by introducing yourself, asking the patient's preferred name and pronouns, and sitting at eye level facing the patient.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 54-year-old woman comes to her primary care physician for a follow-up visit. When asked what brings her in today, she mentions that her diabetes has been harder to control, that she has been sleeping poorly since her husband died, and that she also noticed some foot numbness. The physician has only 20 minutes and is tempted to focus solely on the glucose log.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Tell the patient that grief counseling is outside the scope of a diabetes follow-up visit
Identify the patient's concerns and develop a joint agenda with her for the visit, deferring items as needed
Proceed with the glucose review first and document the other issues for a future visit without discussing them
Advise the patient that her sleep problems will likely resolve once her hemoglobin A1c improves
Ask the patient to choose the single most important issue and agree to ignore all other concerns this visit

explanation_correct: Agenda setting is the patient-centered interviewing technique in which the physician identifies the patient's concerns and sets goals by developing a joint agenda between the physician and the patient. When a patient raises multiple issues, the appropriate response is to enumerate them together and agree on what will be addressed now versus later, rather than unilaterally selecting the physician's preferred topic or dismissing concerns.

explanation_incorrect.A: Declaring grief counseling out of scope dismisses the patient's concern; the correct approach is to include it in a shared agenda and address or schedule it appropriately.
explanation_incorrect.C: Silently deferring the other issues without discussion is not agenda setting; the patient should participate in prioritizing her concerns.
explanation_incorrect.D: Attributing sleep problems to glycemic control is falsely reassuring and imposes a physician-determined explanation instead of exploring the patient's concerns.
explanation_incorrect.E: Forcing the patient to pick one issue and ignoring the rest abandons the joint agenda; the physician and patient should set goals together, which may include scheduling deferred items.

educationalObjective: Agenda setting means building a joint agenda with the patient by identifying and prioritizing the patient's concerns together.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 38-year-old man describes several weeks of chest discomfort, saying: "Work has been crushing me, my father died last month, and I keep waking up at 3 a.m. with my heart pounding. I don't know if it's my heart or my head." After listening, the physician replies: "So you're under a lot of strain at work and recently lost your father, and the chest symptoms and sleeplessness are happening in the middle of all that — do I have that right?"
question: Which patient-centered interviewing technique is the physician using in this reply?
explanation_correct: Reflection is the technique of actively listening and synthesizing the information offered by the patient, particularly with respect to the primary concern(s). The physician restates and connects the patient's psychosocial strain and somatic symptoms into a coherent summary, checking its accuracy, which demonstrates that the patient has been heard and helps surface the main concern.

explanation_incorrect.A: Facilitation means encouraging the patient to speak freely without guiding or leading questions (eg, "Go on," "Tell me more"), not synthesizing what was said.
explanation_incorrect.B: Validation legitimizes or affirms the patient's perspectives (eg, "It makes sense that this worries you"), which the physician has not done in this reply.
explanation_incorrect.C: Agenda setting is identifying concerns and building a joint agenda at the start of the visit; this reply occurs mid-interview and summarizes rather than prioritizes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Recapitulation is summarizing what the patient has said so far to ensure correct interpretation, typically later in the interview after a longer narrative; here the physician is synthesizing the primary concern in real time, which is reflection.

educationalObjective: Reflection is actively listening and synthesizing the patient's narrative, especially around the primary concern.

subject: PHS
vignette: During a new patient visit, a 67-year-old woman has told a long, detailed story about her symptoms, her late husband's illness, and her recent move to live near her daughter. The physician pauses and says: "Let me make sure I've understood you. You moved two months ago, your symptoms started around the same time, and you're worried about managing on your own — is that an accurate picture?"
question: Which patient-centered interviewing technique is the physician demonstrating?
explanation_correct: Recapitulation is summarizing what the patient has said so far to ensure correct interpretation. After a lengthy narrative, the physician condenses the key points and explicitly checks that the summary is accurate, which prevents misunderstanding and signals close attention to the patient's story.

explanation_incorrect.B: Validation legitimizes or affirms the patient's perspectives; the physician here is summarizing content, not affirming the patient's viewpoint.
explanation_incorrect.C: Facilitation involves encouraging the patient to speak freely without leading questions (eg, nodding, "please continue"), not restating the narrative.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reflection synthesizes information, particularly around the primary concern, as the patient is speaking; here the physician is condensing and verifying an entire narrative after the fact.
explanation_incorrect.E: Agenda setting is the process of identifying concerns and developing joint goals for the visit, which has not occurred in this exchange.

educationalObjective: Recapitulation means summarizing the patient's story and verifying that your interpretation is correct.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 45-year-old man becomes tearful while telling his physician that he has been unable to return to work since a motor vehicle accident. He says, "I know I'm probably overreacting, but I just can't make myself drive." The physician replies: "It's completely understandable that you feel this way after what you went through — many people in your situation feel the same."
question: Which element of the PEARLS rapport framework is the physician using?
explanation_correct: Legitimization, the second L in PEARLS, means assuring the patient that emotional responses are understandable or common. By telling the patient that his reaction is completely understandable and shared by others in his situation, the physician directly normalizes and legitimizes his distress, countering the patient's belief that he is "overreacting."

explanation_incorrect.A: Partnership means working together with the patient to identify primary concerns and develop preferred solutions; the physician has not proposed working together on a solution.
explanation_incorrect.B: Empathy means acknowledging the emotions displayed and demonstrating understanding of why the patient feels that way; the statement here goes beyond acknowledgment to declare the feeling normal, which is legitimization.
explanation_incorrect.C: Apology means taking personal responsibility when appropriate; there is no error or responsibility to accept in this scenario.
explanation_incorrect.D: Respect means commending the patient for constructive behaviors such as coming in to discuss a problem or pushing through difficult circumstances; the physician has not offered such commendation.

educationalObjective: Legitimization in PEARLS is assuring the patient that their emotional response is understandable or common.
